title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 11-15
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 11-15 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A workflow finishes, reports success, and produces a wrong figure with nothing flagged. Which failure does that describe?
options: A silent error, where the run fails without surfacing any warning
A hallucination, where generated text cites a source that does not exist
A mid-flow break, where the run stops before its final step
A rollback, where the workflow returns to an earlier version
questions.explanation: A silent error is defined by the absence of a signal: the process completes and reports success while the result is wrong. Loud failures announce themselves, so this kind has to be caught by checking the output rather than the status.

questions.question: A tool writes a fluent paragraph with a citation to a source. What check actually catches fabrication?
options: Asking the tool whether the citation is accurate
Checking the specific claim against the original source
Re-running the same prompt and comparing the two outputs
Judging whether the paragraph reads confidently and smoothly
questions.explanation: Confidence is the tell, not the evidence: fluent text can surround an invented citation. Only verifying the specific claim against a source you can inspect separates real support from fabricated support.

questions.question: A workflow breaks midway after already sending one message. What makes a retry safe?
options: It restarts from the beginning so every single run is identical
It skips the failed step and reports the run as complete
It resumes where it stopped, so done work does not repeat
It waits for a person to redo each step by hand
questions.explanation: A retry is safe when repeating it produces no additional side effects, so work that already happened is not done twice. Restarting blindly duplicates the completed step, which is the harm a safe re-run is designed to avoid.

questions.question: A report feeds a decision that is made once a week. What cadence fits it best?
options: A weekly run timed to finish before the decision is made
An hourly run so the figures are always as fresh as possible
A daily run so a full week of data is never out of date
A run every time the source data changes, regardless of use
questions.explanation: Cadence should match how often the output is actually used, not how fast it could run. A weekly decision needs a run timed before it, and more frequent runs spend effort on results nobody consumes.

questions.question: What distinguishes a triggered run from a scheduled run?
options: It runs more often than a scheduled job and always produces fresher output
It processes items in a group rather than one at a time
It requires a person to approve the output before delivery
It starts because an event occurred rather than at a set clock time
questions.explanation: A scheduled run starts on the clock whether or not anything changed, while a triggered run starts because an event happened. That difference is also why a quiet day produces no run at all when the start is event driven.

questions.question: Two hundred submissions land in one hour and the workflow cannot keep pace. What does a queue do?
options: It processes the whole pile at once so the backlog clears immediately
It drops the excess items so the workflow stays within capacity
It lines work up in arrival order and clears it at a steady pace
It converts the schedule into an event trigger for future runs
questions.explanation: A queue absorbs the gap between how fast work arrives and how fast it can be handled, holding items in order until they are processed. Handling the spike all at once or dropping items is the failure a queue exists to prevent.

questions.question: Which characteristic of a step best justifies a mandatory approval before it continues?
options: The step is routine, reversible, and has behaved the same way for months
The action is hard to undo and the output goes outside the team
The step is fast and cheap, so pausing it costs almost nothing
The step produces a draft that no one reads until the following week
questions.explanation: A gate earns its interruption where a miss is costly: hard-to-undo actions, low confidence, outside visibility, or context the tool lacks. Routine and reversible steps earn rhythm instead, because gating them rebuilds the bottleneck automation removed.

questions.question: What distinguishes human-in-the-loop oversight from human-on-the-loop oversight?
options: A person watches a dashboard and steps in only when an exception appears
A person checks the output after the workflow has already finished
A person must approve the output before the workflow can continue
A person builds the workflow and then leaves it to run untouched
questions.explanation: In the loop means the human decision sits inside the path, so nothing proceeds until someone authorizes it. On the loop means the workflow executes on its own while a person watches and intervenes afterward.

questions.question: A gate approved cleanly for months starts getting signed off without a real read. What is the structural defense?
options: Add a second approval step from the same reviewer on every run
Remove the gate, since a reliable workflow no longer needs one
Run the workflow less often so each review feels more significant
Put the deciding evidence in front of the reviewer at the gate
questions.explanation: Complacency grows as a system proves reliable, so willpower is a weak defense. Designing the pause so the evidence needed to decide arrives in one place, and the check cannot be bypassed, makes a genuine review the easiest path.

questions.question: What does dividing a prompt into labeled sections actually accomplish?
options: It lets the model and a reader tell rules from context and data
It makes the prompt shorter and cheaper to send on every single run
It removes any need to test the prompt after it is changed
It lets the same prompt run on any model without further edits
questions.explanation: Structure marks which text is instruction, which is context, and which is variable input, so the model reads each part correctly and a reader can see where to edit. The gain is legibility and safe editing, not brevity or portability.

questions.question: What makes a why-line beside a rule worth writing?
options: It repeats the instruction in different words so the model notices it
It records why the rule exists so a reader can judge if it holds
It proves the rule was written by a person rather than generated
It keeps the rule from being changed without a second approval
questions.explanation: A comment preserves the reason behind a rule, which is the knowledge that disappears first and the thing needed to decide whether the rule can change. Restating the rule adds no information, and duplicating it couples the parts.

questions.question: What is the warning sign that a prompt's rules have become coupled?
options: The prompt runs longer than a single screen of text
The variable input sits in its own clearly labeled slot, apart from the rules
One rule appears in several sentences, so one edit touches them all
The prompt uses a delimiter that the model does not recognize
questions.explanation: Coupling means one logical rule lives in multiple places, so a single intended change forces several edits and a missed one leaves the prompt contradicting itself. Stating each rule once, in one home, is what makes an edit safe.

questions.question: Where do multi-step pipelines most often fail?
options: Inside the most complex step, where the prompt does the hardest work
At the handoff, where one step's output does not fit the next
At the trigger, because scheduled runs start at the wrong moment
At the final output, because the posting tool rejects formatted content
questions.explanation: Each step is built to consume a particular shape of input, so a change in what the previous step produces breaks the next one at the join. Naming every handoff is what turns a mysterious failure into a located one.

questions.question: What does naming each boundary buy when you assemble a pipeline?
options: It removes the need for any human review gate anywhere in the flow
It makes the pipeline run faster because steps can overlap
It exposes a broken join at a named boundary, not downstream
It guarantees that no step will produce unexpected output
questions.explanation: Writing down what a step produces and what the next step needs makes the interface explicit. When a shape changes, the failure appears at the boundary you named rather than as odd behavior blamed on the wrong step.

questions.question: A job will run once and never again. What does the assembly guidance say?
options: Build it as a pipeline anyway so the work is documented formally
Add extra steps now so individual parts can be reused later
Automate the trigger but leave the remaining steps manual
Keep it simple, since the handoffs add cost with no payback
questions.explanation: Assembly earns its cost when a job recurs with a stable shape and each step removes manual work. For a one-off, every added handoff is another thing that can break with nothing to repay it.
